questions.a: 'swimming' — 'enjoy' takes gerunds only. A wrong answer 'to swim' shows the universal-infinitive habit.

questions.q: 'She stopped ___ (smoke).' = she quit the habit. Which form?
questions.a: 'smoking' — gerund = the stopped activity. 'to smoke' would mean she paused in order to smoke — the opposite meaning. The flip is the whole lesson.
'to lock' — a future task needs the infinitive ('don't forget to'). 'Locking' would mean recalling a past act of locking.

questions.q: Some verbs insist on gerunds (enjoy, avoid, finish, mind, suggest), some insist on ______ (want, decide, promise, learn, agree), and a few take both with meaning shifts (stop smoking ≠ stop to smoke; remember doing ≠ remember to do).

Fill in the blank: Some verbs insist on gerunds (enjoy, avoid, finish, mind, suggest), some insist on ______ (want, decide, promise, learn, agree), and a few take both with meaning shifts (stop smoking ≠ stop to smoke; remember doing ≠ remember to do).

Fill in the blank: The meaning-flips are the treasure: 'He stopped smoking' = quit the habit; 'He stopped to smoke' = paused in order to smoke — ______ actions. 'Remember to lock' = don't forget (future task); 'remember locking' = recall the past act.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student supplies the correct non-finite after common verbs, applies the preference lists, and explains meaning-flips in stop/remember/try + gerund-vs-infinitive pairs.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: The meaning-flips are the ______: 'He stopped smoking' = quit the habit; 'He stopped to smoke' = paused in order to smoke — opposite actions. 'Remember to lock' = don't forget (future task); 'remember locking' = recall the past act.
